question: Honeywell reported Q2 2026 a few weeks after spinning off Aerospace. What were consolidated sales vs sales excluding Aerospace, and why is GAAP EPS from continuing operations so far above adjusted EPS?
grading: Use HON, CIK 773840. Consolidated sales USD 9,719M; ex-Aerospace sales USD 5,187M. Identify the Quantinuum gain removal (-$15.87/share) as the main EPS adjustment. State actual Q2 close June 27, spin June 29 in Q3, and Aerospace consolidated in Q2 with discontinued-operations presentation beginning Q3. Keep consolidated and ex-Aerospace EPS bases distinct.
answer: HON consolidated Q2 2026 sales were USD 9,719 million; sales excluding Aerospace were USD 5,187 million. Consolidated GAAP continuing-operations EPS of $17.83 reconciles to adjusted EPS of $4.52, principally by removing $15.87 per share of Quantinuum deconsolidation gains; other net adjustments add $2.56. Ex-Aerospace EPS was $16.65 GAAP / $1.95 adjusted. The Q2 actual close was June 27, although presented as June 30: the June 29 Aerospace spin occurred in Q3. Aerospace remains consolidated in this Q2 presentation and becomes discontinued operations beginning Q3. [G25-E1, G25-E2]

output.answer:
Based on the available information, here's what Honeywell reported for Q2 2026 following the June 29, 2026 spin-off of Honeywell Aerospace:

## Consolidated vs. Excluding Aerospace Sales

| Metric | Amount |
|--------|--------|
| **Total/consolidated sales** (including Aerospace through June 29) | **~$9.7 billion** |
| **Sales excluding Aerospace** (Honeywell Technologies continuing operations) | **~$5.2 billion** |
| Aerospace Technologies segment sales (included for ~2 months pre-spin) | ~$4.5 billion |

Because the spin-off closed near quarter-end, Q2 GAAP results included roughly two months of Aerospace operations within the consolidated entity. The "standalone" Honeywell Technologies pure-play automation business reported approximately **$5.2 billion** in sales, up ~3% YoY (and ~4% organically). [Source](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/honeywell-technologies-beats-second-quarter-123700077.html)

## Why GAAP EPS From Continuing Operations Is Far Above Adjusted EPS

**The short answer:** A massive one-time accounting gain on the Aerospace spin-off was recorded in **continuing operations** under GAAP, while adjusted/normalized EPS strips that gain out.

According to coverage of the results, GAAP diluted EPS surged to roughly **~$17.83** (on net income of ~$5.68 billion), compared to adjusted EPS of around **$1.95** for the quarter. [Source](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/investors-reacting-honeywell-hon-eps-151027061.html)

Key drivers of the gap:

1. **Spin-off remeasurement/distribution gain.** Under U.S. GAAP (ASC 845), when a subsidiary is distributed to shareholders in a spin-off, it is typically remeasured to fair value. Because Honeywell Aerospace's fair value significantly exceeded its carrying/book value on Honeywell's balance sheet, the company recognized a large non-cash gain in continuing operations upon distribution. This is a non-recurring accounting event, not operational profit.

2. **Transaction-related items.** The quarter also included other one-time separation effects and stranded-cost adjustments tied to the carve-out.

Analyst commentary explicitly noted that investors were being asked to "look past a smaller revenue base, **one-time gains**, stranded costs, and a wobbly aerospace sibling" to assess the underlying business. [Source](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/honeywell-slides-5-future-growth-185552794.html)

**Bottom line:** The ~9x gap between reported GAAP EPS (~$17.83) and adjusted EPS (~$1.95) has nothing to do with operating performance. It reflects a non-cash accounting gain on the Aerospace separation that analysts and management exclude when evaluating the continuing automation business.
